questions.title: Microservices vs Monolith
questions.question: What are microservices and when should you choose them over a monolith?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- **Microservices: independently deployable services around business capabilities**
- **Monolith-first: start monolithic, extract when pain is real and team is larger**
- **Microservices win: independent scaling, independent deployments, team autonomy**
- **Microservices cost: distributed complexity — network failures, data consistency, observability**
- **Conway's Law: system architecture mirrors team structure**
- **Red flag:** choosing microservices for a team of 2 — operational overhead kills velocity

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Microservices decompose an application into independently deployable services, each owning its own data store and business capability. The key trade-off is that you gain independent scaling, deployment, and team autonomy at the cost of distributed systems complexity: network failures, eventual consistency, cross-service tracing, and operational overhead.

For a small team or early-stage product, a well-structured monolith is almost always the right choice — it's easier to refactor, test, deploy, and reason about. Microservices make sense when you have multiple teams stepping on each other's deployments, when different parts of the system have dramatically different scaling needs, or when you need to use different technology stacks for different capabilities.

The classic guidance: start with a monolith, identify seams where services naturally want to form, and extract when the pain of staying monolithic outweighs the cost of distribution.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Monolith vs Microservices — Honest Comparison

```
Dimension           | Monolith              | Microservices
--------------------|-----------------------|---------------------------
Deployment          | One artifact          | 10s or 100s of services
Development speed   | Fast initially        | Slower start, scales well
Testing             | Simpler (in-process)  | Complex (inter-service)
Debugging           | Stack trace           | Distributed tracing
Data consistency    | ACID transactions     | Eventual consistency
Scaling             | Scale entire app      | Scale hot services only
Team structure      | One team feasible     | Team per service (Conway)
Infrastructure      | Simple                | Service mesh, registries
Local development   | One process           | Docker Compose / minikube
Operational cost    | Low                   | High (Kubernetes, mesh)
```

## When Microservices Make Sense

```
GOOD INDICATORS:
  ✓ Multiple teams (5+ developers per domain)
  ✓ Different scaling requirements:
    - Search service: CPU-heavy, needs 20 instances
    - Auth service: low traffic, 2 instances fine
    - Upload service: I/O heavy, needs more disk
  ✓ Different release cadences:
    - Core order service: monthly release (stable)
    - Recommendation service: weekly releases
  ✓ Technology diversity justified:
    - ML model service in Python
    - High-performance matching engine in Go
    - Core business logic in Java
  ✓ Compliance isolation:
    - Payment processing needs PCI scope isolation
    - GDPR-sensitive user data separate from analytics

WARNING SIGNS:
  ✗ Team of 3 people with 10 microservices
  ✗ All services deployed together anyway
  ✗ Distributed monolith (services tightly coupled via sync calls)
  ✗ Shared database across services
  ✗ No observability (logging, tracing, metrics) in place
```

## Service Boundary Design — Domain-Driven

```java
// WRONG: Technical layers as services
service: UserDataService     // All user data access
service: EmailService        // All email sending
service: DatabaseService     // Shared DB access

// RIGHT: Business capabilities as services
service: OrderService        // Order placement, order management
service: InventoryService    // Stock levels, reservations
service: PaymentService      // Payment processing, refunds
service: NotificationService // Email, SMS, push notifications
service: UserService         // User profiles, preferences

// Each service:
//   - Has its OWN database (no shared DB!)
//   - Owns its domain entities end-to-end
//   - Exposes an API (REST or events)
//   - Can be deployed independently
```

## Data Ownership Rule

```
CRITICAL RULE: Each service owns its data.
No direct DB queries from Service A into Service B's DB.

WRONG:
OrderService → SELECT * FROM users WHERE user_id = ?  (UserService's DB!)

RIGHT:
OrderService → GET /api/users/42 (UserService's API)
             OR
OrderService caches the user info it needs at order creation time
             OR
OrderService subscribes to UserUpdatedEvent to keep local copy

Reason: if two services share a DB, they're not independent —
schema change in shared DB breaks both, defeats the purpose.
```

## Production Reality

For an interview, a good answer acknowledges both sides. You've worked in a monolith, you know the benefits (simplicity, easy refactoring). You understand microservices trade-offs and would only advocate for them when team size and operational maturity justify the complexity. Mentioning Conway's Law — that your architecture will reflect your team communication structure — shows architectural maturity.
